issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette:
Aung was 77, a retired surgeon born to a South Eastern Asian family and still living with his wife in the same house where he had tried, for years, to keep himself orderly and useful. His difficulties traced back to a night in the operating theatre decades earlier, when he had been called in to witness a catastrophic burn injury after an industrial accident. He remembered the smell first: burnt tissue and singed clothing that seemed to cling to the room long after the patient had been taken away. The skin temperature on his own hands that night, heated under the surgical lights and slick beneath gloves, had lodged in his mind in a way he could not explain. Even now, a particular warmth on his skin-an overheated room, a bath that is too hot, sunlight trapped against his forearm-could pull him back to that night with startling force, and stress in any form made the reaction sharper. On difficult days he felt abruptly jumpy, bracing at unexpected or loud sounds, and he would scan the environment before he could stop himself, as if danger might arrive in the next second. He had come to believe that his body kept reacting as if it were still in danger even when he was safe, and that there was something wrong with him as a person for not simply being able to leave it behind. That conviction fed a constant sense that he had to be especially careful because one never knew what could happen next.

Over time, those appraisals shaped how he lived. Aung began trying hard not to think about the event at all, and when the memories pushed in, he pushed away any positive feeling that came with family visits, a good meal, or a quiet afternoon, because even comfort felt unsafe to him, as if letting himself relax would make him vulnerable. He also avoided television programmes, films, and articles about accidents, hospitals, or fires, and his wife had noticed that he would change the channel quickly if a scene included smoke or a hospital corridor. In his retirement routine, he became cautious in ways that sometimes looked almost reckless to others: he took too many risks on short errands, walking faster than was sensible or ignoring his own fatigue, as though he needed to prove he was still in control. Yet the same vigilance that drove those actions also made him pull back from ordinary life. A faint burnt smell from a neighbour's cooking on the apartment stairwell, or the stress of a family disagreement, could set him on edge and send him back to his effort to suppress the memory.

What Aung found most unsettling was that the memory did not always arrive as a clear scene. At times it came stripped of image, only the full emotional intensity breaking over him-fear, helplessness, and the tense nausea of that night-without a coherent picture to hold onto. When fragments did surface, they felt strangely alien, as if the event belonged to someone else rather than to him, and the sequence of what had happened was confused and difficult to put in order. He would try to force the pieces into place, but the more he strained, the more disjointed they became. Those gaps deepened his belief that something was wrong with him, and that his body's reactions meant he remained unsafe in the present. The result was a tightening loop: when his body jumped at a sudden sound or a hot draft against his skin, he became more focused on danger, and that hyperalert state would bring the memory closer again. Once it was there, he reacted by trying not to think, by shutting down feeling, by turning away from anything resembling the event, but those efforts rarely settled him for long.

As weeks and months passed, the things he avoided became more potent rather than less. The more he stayed away from films, news reports, and even conversations about injuries, the more starkly the burnt smell in the stairwell or the sudden heat from a kettle could seize him. Because he kept pushing away the memory and any comfort tied to it, the emotional force would return in raw waves, and each wave seemed to confirm that his body could not be trusted. He had gradually become more watchful in the home he shared with his wife, pausing at odd noises, listening for unexpected sounds in the night, and feeling compelled to stay alert in a way that exhausted him. His wife described him as present but distant, less able to enjoy the warmth of grandchildren's visits, and Aung admitted that he often cut those moments short before they could feel too good. Only recently, after a particularly intense episode in which a sudden burnt smell at breakfast left him trembling and unable to settle for hours, did he agree to seek help. He came now because he was afraid the jumpiness, the avoidance, and the sense that something was wrong with him would keep narrowing his life, and because a part of him still hoped he might learn how to feel safe in his own body again.
